views.title: Native lifecycle
views.question: What happens after I run ascii-chat?
views.goal: Trace mode dispatch, shared setup, rendering ownership, and ordered teardown.
views.subtitle: Trace mode dispatch, shared setup, rendering ownership, and ordered teardown.
views.outcome: Distinguish mode callbacks from shared infrastructure and follow startup through to shutdown.
views.diagnostic: Separate option validation, capture creation, connection setup, and the first displayed frame when startup stalls.

chapters.title: Choose a mode
chapters.summary: One executable dispatches to one mode; it does not run every mode loop.

steps.title: Dispatch through the mode table
steps.text: The binary registers server, client, mirror, discovery-service, and implicit discovery entry points. The selected entry point determines the rest of the lifecycle.

steps.title: Resolve the invocation
steps.text: Mode detection determines how positional arguments are interpreted. Configuration, environment values, and explicit flags are resolved before the mode consumes settings.

steps.title: Install a mode callback
steps.text: Mirror delegates to the client-like lifecycle. Compare client_main and discovery_main: shared setup is retained while connection and run callbacks change.

chapters.title: Own the session
chapters.summary: Shared contexts establish media and output ownership before the mode runs.

steps.title: Coordinate setup
steps.text: The lifecycle coordinates capture, display, splash, audio, and session attempts. Mode-specific preparation and run callbacks supply the differences.

steps.title: Select a frame source
steps.text: Capture abstracts webcam, file, test pattern, and network-fed media while retaining source dimensions, timing, and ownership.

steps.title: Select an output target
steps.text: Display owns terminal capabilities, dimensions, output policy, and optional render-file state.

chapters.title: Run and release
chapters.summary: Leaving a render loop is only one part of shutdown.

steps.title: Choose the scheduler
steps.text: Local capture can use the pipeline; callback-driven modes provide capture and sleep callbacks. Snapshot completion and exit checks belong here.

steps.title: Interrupt workers
steps.text: Protocol reception, capture, audio, and keepalive work must stop using resources before their contexts are released.

steps.title: Release shared resources
steps.text: Cleanup detaches capture/audio, completes render-file output, destroys display state, and restores terminal/logging behavior.

views.title: Browser → ASCII
views.question: How does a browser use the same ASCII engine as the CLI?
views.goal: Follow browser pixels through TypeScript memory adapters, C/WASM conversion, and terminal rasterization.
views.subtitle: Follow browser pixels through TypeScript memory adapters, C/WASM conversion, and terminal rasterization.
views.outcome: Identify who captures pixels, who generates ASCII, and how ANSI becomes canvas pixels.
views.diagnostic: A blank preview can originate in media acquisition, WASM initialization, zero grid dimensions, or presentation.

chapters.title: Prepare the browser
chapters.summary: React composes sources and waits for a usable WASM module and grid.

steps.title: Compose the preview
steps.text: The page supplies initialization, settings, media selection, and renderer refs instead of implementing another ASCII converter.

steps.title: Wait for readiness
steps.text: WASM readiness and terminal dimensions gate settings and rendering. A ready camera does not imply valid C renderer dimensions.

steps.title: Acquire browser frames
steps.text: The browser owns camera permissions and video/canvas elements. File playback is a separate source feeding the same render loop.

chapters.title: Cross into C
chapters.summary: Browser scheduling calls exported C functions instead of entering a native blocking loop.

steps.title: Schedule conversion
steps.text: The loop checks dimensions/readiness and obtains frames at browser media cadence.

steps.title: Marshal memory
steps.text: The wrapper moves frame bytes into WASM and reads returned ASCII. Allocation, string ownership, and release belong to this boundary.

steps.title: Use the C renderer
steps.text: The exported entry point applies dimensions, options, filters, and animation before reusable C conversion.

chapters.title: Present the result
chapters.summary: ANSI is an intermediate representation, not the final browser image.

steps.title: Feed shared UI state
steps.text: The handle sends media, keys, and resize events through the C UI session before presenting tick output.

steps.title: Create the terminal renderer
steps.text: Font loading, renderer lifetime, resize handling, and canvas initialization belong to this hook.

steps.title: Rasterize terminal text
steps.text: libvterm interprets ANSI; glyph rendering generates a pixel surface. This is distinct from the camera-to-ASCII conversion.

views.title: Browser networking
views.question: What does Connect actually start?
views.goal: Separate UI orchestration, session strategy, browser transport, and C protocol/crypto state.
views.subtitle: Separate UI orchestration, session strategy, browser transport, and C protocol/crypto state.
views.outcome: Trace direct server connections separately from joining or hosting a discovered session.
views.diagnostic: An open signaling WebSocket is a different milestone from a protocol-ready peer media channel.

chapters.title: Select a session
chapters.summary: One client page supports different connection strategies.

steps.title: Collect intent
steps.text: ClientPage composes media, security, connection controls, and rendering. DiscoveryPage simply enables discovery mode.

steps.title: Choose the strategy
steps.text: The hook creates ClientConnection for direct access, WebRTCSession for joining, or BrowserHostSession for creation. Reconnect policy follows this choice.

steps.title: Use one contract
steps.text: ClientSession supplies connect/disconnect, packet send, and state callbacks without requiring one transport implementation.

chapters.title: Cross the protocol boundary
chapters.summary: Browser adapters own sockets and scheduling while reusable C code owns protocol and crypto operations.

steps.title: Drive socket events
steps.text: This class feeds browser transport events into C/WASM client state and must propagate transport failures rather than trust stale module state.

steps.title: Adapt exported APIs
steps.text: The module exposes packet helpers, crypto operations, and client state to TypeScript. Socket bytes cross this interface.

steps.title: Initialize C state
steps.text: Exports initialize options/state and handle handshakes, packet processing, encryption, and outgoing media.

chapters.title: Start media
chapters.summary: Connected state is followed by capability and stream-control packets.

steps.title: Advertise capabilities
steps.text: CLIENT_CAPABILITIES and STREAM_START use actual renderer dimensions, settings, and codec support.

steps.title: Wait for host readiness
steps.text: The initial SERVER_STATE acknowledges native host registration; a DataChannel open event can precede installation of the host receive callback.

steps.title: Manage media producers
steps.text: Video and audio send through the selected session. Disconnect stops producers before closing a channel they might still use.

views.title: Shared UI runtime
views.question: How do help, splash, logs, and video share a screen?
views.goal: Trace native and browser input into shared C screen state and composed output.
views.subtitle: Trace native and browser input into shared C screen state and composed output.
views.outcome: Distinguish host scheduling adapters from C behavior that chooses and draws screens.
views.diagnostic: Follow a key through input, returned action, UI tick, terminal feed, and presentation when visible state fails to change.

chapters.title: Route input
chapters.summary: Native and browser hosts adapt events into shared C behavior.

steps.title: Handle native keys
steps.text: Application actions and setting changes are routed with controller ownership of the current screen.

steps.title: Handle browser keys
steps.text: The handle forwards keyboard, dimensions, logs, and media to SessionUi and applies returned host actions.

steps.title: Own one UI instance
steps.text: This wrapper allocates event strings and owns one C UI session, rather than owning the complete WASM module.

chapters.title: Choose and draw
chapters.summary: Shared nonblocking C state avoids independent React replicas of native screens.

steps.title: Expose host-driven ticks
steps.text: WASM exports forward time, input, loading, media, and resize into the shared session.

steps.title: Advance screen state
steps.text: Animation, dirty flags, help, loading, logs, and media determine the composed output.

steps.title: Compose screen cells
steps.text: Shared frame buffers hold terminal output. Native controller composition also uses these rendering facilities.

chapters.title: Deliver the frame
chapters.summary: Native terminals and browser canvases diverge after the shared UI produces text.

steps.title: Present natively
steps.text: Display combines terminal capabilities, controller updates, and media output. Resizing changes upstream rendering dimensions.

steps.title: Present in a browser
steps.text: C UI output feeds the terminal rasterizer, whose pixels are copied into the canvas.

steps.title: Read the pixel surface
steps.text: The terminal renderer exposes pixels, pitch, and dimensions. It is not a second ASCII conversion algorithm.

views.title: Discovery service
views.question: What does ACDS do for a call?
views.goal: Follow service startup, database membership, request dispatch, signaling, and expiration.
views.subtitle: Follow service startup, database membership, request dispatch, signaling, and expiration.
views.outcome: Separate naming/membership from the peer media host and find the relay and persistence handlers.
views.diagnostic: A valid session name is not proof of media connectivity. Check join results, host availability, signaling, and media transport separately.

chapters.title: Start ACDS
chapters.summary: The service uses server-like lifecycle infrastructure with discovery-specific callbacks.

steps.title: Configure the mode
steps.text: Identity, database settings, and callbacks are assembled before entering the shared server lifecycle.

steps.title: Own service state
steps.text: Startup opens persistent session state and rate limiting. Maintenance handles expiry, old rate-limit records, and migrations.

steps.title: Identify the endpoint
steps.text: The signaling endpoint has its own loaded/generated identity, separate from participant camera streams.

chapters.title: Persist membership
chapters.summary: Create, lookup, join, and leave produce database-backed protocol results.

steps.title: Run the shared protocol
steps.text: Native and browser adapters enter the same C protocol state machine with creation/join intent and credentials.

steps.title: Dispatch requests
steps.text: ACIP dispatch validates packet structure and forwards discovery operations to service callbacks.

steps.title: Record the participant
steps.text: The database resolves sessions, verifies join requirements, records members, and tracks the host. Expiration and leave alter this state.

chapters.title: Relay control traffic
chapters.summary: ACDS carries negotiation and coordination; media has another transport and host.

steps.title: Route SDP and ICE
steps.text: Participant-addressed signaling connects membership knowledge to peer negotiation.

steps.title: Emit native signaling
steps.text: Callbacks associate descriptions/candidates with session and recipient identifiers before sending through discovery transport.

steps.title: Keep media on the peer channel
steps.text: Browser signaling stays on ACDS while media travels on the peer DataChannel. Their reconnection milestones differ.

columnTitles: Keep media on the peer channel

views.title: Host a call
views.question: I want to start a call and invite someone.
views.goal: Compare a dedicated CLI server with a discovered browser host, then follow admission and shared media.
views.subtitle: Compare a dedicated CLI server with a discovered browser host, then follow admission and shared media.
views.outcome: Find the owner of the listener, session name, participant state, and outgoing composites.
views.diagnostic: If the invite exists but the picture does not, check admission and incoming participant frames before ASCII conversion.

chapters.title: Choose a host model
chapters.summary: Dedicated-server and browser-created calls have different startup adapters.

steps.title: Start a dedicated server
steps.text: server_main installs server callbacks into session_server_like_run. Its multi-client render/protocol pipeline remains in src/server.

steps.title: Select browser creation
steps.text: Discovery with createSession selects BrowserHostSession instead of the joining strategy; UI state receives the resulting session name.

steps.title: Create the browser host
steps.text: The adapter opens signaling, enters discovery in create mode, and initializes C hosting after membership is known. It owns browser peers and scheduling.

chapters.title: Admit participants
chapters.summary: Acceptance, security readiness, and media membership are separate steps.

steps.title: Accept native TCP
steps.text: The event-driven native path attaches clients and feeds input to server protocol/security handling.

steps.title: Attach a browser transport
steps.text: The export allocates a C host client and installs callbacks sending bytes into JavaScript. It does not create an operating-system listening socket.

steps.title: Register media membership
steps.text: Shared hosting tracks per-client state for browser/discovered hosts. Transport adapters reuse this media host instead of duplicating it.

chapters.title: Render and distribute
chapters.summary: The chosen host model determines which render implementation drives outgoing frames.

steps.title: Render dedicated-server output
steps.text: A per-client worker asks stream.c to build an appropriate composite and ASCII frame.

steps.title: Tick browser hosting
steps.text: Browser scheduling calls this export to render shared C host state. WebCodecs decodes incoming compressed media before C receives RGBA frames.

steps.title: Render shared-host output
steps.text: The reusable host gathers participant media and distributes output through installed transports. A local host can inject its own frames and audio.

views.title: Join a named session
views.question: Someone sent me a session name. How do I join?
views.goal: Follow a shared name through discovery intent, lookup/join, host assignment, and media readiness.
views.subtitle: Follow a shared name through discovery intent, lookup/join, host assignment, and media readiness.
views.outcome: Locate name validation, password rejection, participant assignment, and transition from signaling to a media host.
views.diagnostic: A rejected session/password differs from a negotiation timeout. Terminal discovery rejection should not be treated like transient media failure.

chapters.title: Resolve the invite
chapters.summary: CLI and browser entry points collect the identifier before starting discovery.

steps.title: Enter native discovery
steps.text: The mode installs discovery preparation and run callbacks into the client-like lifecycle. Implicit discovery dispatch reaches this entry point.

steps.title: Reuse browser client UI
steps.text: DiscoveryPage renders ClientPage with discoveryMode; media and connection controls are shared rather than reimplemented.

steps.title: Marshal joining credentials
steps.text: The browser allocates name/password strings, calls C discovery exports, and forwards queued outgoing packets after returning from C.

chapters.title: Look up and join
chapters.summary: The shared C protocol sequences requests and interprets service responses.

steps.title: Choose the entry flow
steps.text: Creation and joining are explicit protocol intents. Lookup/join responses advance the same state machine.

steps.title: Join from native code
steps.text: The native adapter consumes membership responses, stores participant and host details, and transitions toward negotiation.

steps.title: Accept or reject membership
steps.text: The service verifies the session and join requirements, records participation, and supplies information needed to reach the host.

chapters.title: Become a media participant
chapters.summary: Database membership is followed by transport establishment and protocol readiness.

steps.title: Start discovery processing
steps.text: The session connects to ACDS and runs create/join work. An initiator also joins its created session to receive participant notifications.

steps.title: Establish the browser peer
steps.text: The joining adapter exchanges signaling and waits for host protocol acknowledgement before declaring media readiness.

steps.title: Install native transport ownership
steps.text: Discovery can attach an already-negotiated transport. Capture and playback then use that transport instead of repeating discovery.

views.title: Connect to a server
views.question: I have a server address instead of a session name.
views.goal: Trace direct native TCP and browser WebSocket connections into server admission and common ACIP framing.
views.subtitle: Trace direct native TCP and browser WebSocket connections into server admission and common ACIP framing.
views.outcome: Identify endpoint resolution, socket/channel ownership, security negotiation, and stream-control startup.
views.diagnostic: Connection refused belongs to endpoint/listener setup; an open connection without frames points later to security, capabilities, stream start, or incoming media.

chapters.title: Select an endpoint
chapters.summary: A browser uses the WebSocket endpoint, not the CLI raw TCP socket.

steps.title: Configure the CLI client
steps.text: Client mode supplies connection/run callbacks around shared lifecycle setup.

steps.title: Connect natively
steps.text: Connection attempts produce the transport bound to client state. Retry timing and remote errors are recorded independently.

steps.title: Open a browser WebSocket
steps.text: Direct browser access uses a WebSocket adapter and advances C/WASM protocol/security state as bytes arrive.

chapters.title: Accept and secure
chapters.summary: TCP events and WebSocket admission converge on per-client protocol state.

steps.title: Own server listeners
steps.text: Shared lifecycle creates TCP/WebSocket infrastructure, status work, optional discovery advertisement, and shutdown coordination.

steps.title: Admit WebSocket clients
steps.text: The handler attaches a transport and finishes security negotiation before starting media workers. Transport TLS affects application-crypto policy.

steps.title: Admit TCP clients
steps.text: The native event path processes acceptance and queued input without treating every socket as a blocking worker.

chapters.title: Start protocol traffic
chapters.summary: Transport readiness precedes capabilities, streams, and ongoing media packets.

steps.title: Start native reception
steps.text: The client installs ACIP callbacks and starts reception around coordinated capture, audio, terminal dimensions, and keepalive.

steps.title: Frame and validate packets
steps.text: The packet layer carries typed payloads, lengths, sender identity, and integrity data across the chosen transport.

steps.title: Start browser streams
steps.text: After connection readiness, the hook sends capabilities and stream controls. Settings and codec support determine what the server produces.

views.title: Negotiate WebRTC & NAT
views.question: How do callers behind routers reach each other?
views.goal: Follow NAT assessment, STUN/TURN settings, SDP/ICE signaling, and adoption of a media DataChannel.
views.subtitle: Follow NAT assessment, STUN/TURN settings, SDP/ICE signaling, and adoption of a media DataChannel.
views.outcome: Separate candidate discovery, signaling delivery, transport connectivity, and ACIP readiness.
views.diagnostic: Inspect ICE configuration and candidate delivery before packet decoding when Connecting stalls. Browser relay-only mode requires TURN configuration and credentials.

chapters.title: Assess reachability
chapters.summary: Native host selection and browser ICE configuration use different network APIs.

steps.title: Probe native reachability
steps.text: Native probes gather NAT/reachability information used by host selection and negotiation.

steps.title: Choose native roles
steps.text: Negotiation compares quality information to select a connection/host result. This does not itself finish a WebRTC channel.

steps.title: Configure browser ICE
steps.text: STUN/TURN URL schemes, credential pairs, and relay-only requirements are validated before peer connection creation.

chapters.title: Exchange descriptions
chapters.summary: SDP and candidates travel over signaling before media can use the peer channel.

steps.title: Emit native signaling
steps.text: Callbacks package descriptions/candidates with session and recipient identity. Direct signaling can also use an existing control transport.

steps.title: Route peer messages
steps.text: The service delivers participant-addressed signaling. A delivered SDP message alone is not proof of connectivity.

steps.title: Queue peer negotiation
steps.text: Browser code applies remote descriptions and queued ICE while keeping the signaling connection separate from the media channel.

chapters.title: Adopt the channel
chapters.summary: Connected WebRTC bytes become an ACIP transport used by the media session.

steps.title: Wrap native WebRTC
steps.text: The transport adapts send/receive/lifetime behavior to the common ACIP transport interface.

steps.title: Wrap the browser channel
steps.text: DataChannel events become the packet transport contract expected by browser session code; close behavior is handled here.

steps.title: Attach negotiated ownership
steps.text: The native session installs the selected transport in participant state. Browser joining additionally waits for host SERVER_STATE acknowledgement.

views.title: Authenticate & encrypt
views.question: Who am I connected to, and what encrypts the call?
views.goal: Separate secure transport, application encryption, password/key authentication, trust, and rekeying.
views.subtitle: Separate secure transport, application encryption, password/key authentication, trust, and rekeying.
views.outcome: Find policy resolution and both handshake sides without treating TLS, DTLS, and identity verification as interchangeable.
views.diagnostic: Check resolved policy and authentication requirements first. Encrypted transport does not alone establish a verified peer identity.

chapters.title: Resolve policy
chapters.summary: Supplied authentication material and transport security determine ACIP security mode.

steps.title: Resolve application mode
steps.text: Policy considers secure transport, encrypt/no-encrypt flags, passwords, identity, and verification keys. Invalid combinations fail before handshake.

steps.title: Describe browser layers
steps.text: The UI labels WS/WSS signaling, WebRTC DTLS media, and optional application encryption separately. Follow these alongside the selected session strategy.

steps.title: Scope crypto per peer
steps.text: Peer crypto exports support individual peer sessions. A signaling connection is not automatically the media peer identity.

chapters.title: Establish readiness
chapters.summary: Normal media requires the agreed security state to be ready.

steps.title: Drive native client negotiation
steps.text: The adapter coordinates shared handshake logic with the active transport and client error state.

steps.title: Advance server negotiation
steps.text: Per-client security packets advance the server handshake. Failed negotiation prevents media workers from starting.

steps.title: Use the agreed context
steps.text: Shared state supplies packet encryption/decryption after agreement. Browser exports reuse these operations instead of implementing another cipher.

chapters.title: Verify and maintain identity
chapters.summary: Trust records, remote verification keys, and rekeying are different operations.

steps.title: Check remembered keys
steps.text: Known-host records participate in first-use and later identity checks. Inspect this when a previously known server changes keys.

steps.title: Load verification material
steps.text: Remote public-key sources feed key validation and the handshake path. Fetch success is separate from successful peer authentication.

steps.title: Refresh a live context
steps.text: Rekey request/response/completion handlers update key material within the connection lifecycle. They are not a network reconnect.

views.title: Capture & send video
views.question: How does my camera become video packets?
views.goal: Trace acquisition, pacing, size and codec decisions, and raw or encoded upload into a call.
views.subtitle: Trace acquisition, pacing, size and codec decisions, and raw or encoded upload into a call.
views.outcome: Follow native capture and browser WebCodecs upload without confusing outgoing video with local ASCII preview.
views.diagnostic: If preview works but remote video does not, check stream start, upload encoder selection, send queues, and host reception.

chapters.title: Acquire frames
chapters.summary: Native sources and browser media APIs have different device and memory ownership.

steps.title: Read a native source
steps.text: Capture obtains frames from the selected source, tracks dimensions/timing, and exposes them to session code.

steps.title: Run outgoing native capture
steps.text: The worker obtains and processes source frames while honoring connection and stop state. Its output goes to network send helpers.

steps.title: Read browser pixels
steps.text: Canvas capture obtains media-element pixels. Camera permission and device selection stay in browser media hooks.

chapters.title: Select an upload format
chapters.summary: A requested codec is not proof the current browser or receiver supports it.

steps.title: Encode native uploads
steps.text: The session helper obtains a frame and feeds encoder state while tracking codec/frame information.

steps.title: Probe browser encoders
steps.text: Selection probes supported encodings and can try alternatives. Negotiated receiver capability and local API support both matter.

steps.title: Bound WebCodecs work
steps.text: HEVC/AVC configuration is probed; output is Annex B access units. Periodic keyframes and bounded encoder queueing control decoding readiness and latency.

chapters.title: Deliver to a media host
chapters.summary: The host must decode the image before it contributes to anyone’s shared grid.

steps.title: Send native image packets
steps.text: Send helpers package encoded image data through the active transport; raw upload uses a related path.

steps.title: Decode on a native server
steps.text: The protocol validates encoded image payloads and routes them to per-client decoder state.

steps.title: Decode on a browser host
steps.text: WebCodecs produces RGBA frames for shared C hosting. The browser adapter then feeds C host state rather than composing a separate TypeScript grid.

views.title: Receive & render the call
views.question: How do several callers become the picture I see?
views.goal: Follow participant frames, host composition, client-specific ASCII output, packet decode, and final presentation.
views.subtitle: Follow participant frames, host composition, client-specific ASCII output, packet decode, and final presentation.
views.outcome: Locate grid layout, dimensions, palettes, compression, and the last terminal/canvas boundary.
views.diagnostic: Compare source-frame arrival, composite dimensions, receiver capabilities, frame decoding, and renderer readiness when output is blank or incorrectly sized.

chapters.title: Compose participant video
chapters.summary: Dedicated-server composition and shared session-host rendering are distinct implementations.

steps.title: Gather usable frames
steps.text: The dedicated server collects active source frames before single-source or multi-source layout. A connected participant may not have supplied a frame yet.

steps.title: Lay out participants
steps.text: Grid placement and scaling create a composite at the requested dimensions. Different receivers can receive different size/style output.

steps.title: Render shared-host media
steps.text: Discovered/browser hosting renders through shared host state and transport adapters, not the dedicated server’s per-client worker implementation.

chapters.title: Generate ASCII output
chapters.summary: Receiver capabilities affect the composite-to-text conversion and outgoing representation.

steps.title: Render for a receiver
steps.text: The worker requests output for that receiver’s dimensions/settings and queues the frame.

steps.title: Apply the C ASCII engine
steps.text: Palette, color, and style choices feed reusable C rendering. SIMD dispatch chooses available implementations beneath this conversion.

steps.title: Frame the media payload
steps.text: ACIP sends typed media/control data through the chosen transport. Framing and optional compression differ from terminal rasterization.

chapters.title: Decode and present
chapters.summary: Receipt is followed by parsing, decompression, UI composition, and an output target.

steps.title: Decode native frames
steps.text: The native client validates and decodes the received representation before updating display state.

steps.title: Parse browser frame structure
steps.text: The browser frame parser interprets the payload; connection callbacks pass text onward to the renderer.

steps.title: Rasterize browser output
steps.text: ANSI becomes terminal glyph pixels for the canvas. Native display instead writes terminal output through its display/platform path.

views.title: Microphone to speakers
views.question: How do I hear everyone without hearing my own echo?
views.goal: Follow capture, Opus batching, host mixing, playback buffers, device selection, and echo processing.
views.subtitle: Follow capture, Opus batching, host mixing, playback buffers, device selection, and echo processing.
views.outcome: Distinguish missing input, failed upload, an empty mix, decoder problems, and output-device or buffering failures.
views.diagnostic: Follow captured samples, encoded packets, host input, mix-minus output, decoded samples, and speaker playback in order. Volume cannot repair an earlier missing stage.

chapters.title: Capture microphone samples
chapters.summary: Native audio and browser Web Audio produce samples before packetization.

steps.title: Initialize native audio
steps.text: The client configures capture/playback and the shared processing pipeline. Capture and network sending use coordinated workers.

steps.title: Start browser audio
steps.text: AudioContext, microphone streams, saved devices, gain, and playback readiness have browser lifetimes. Generation checks reject stale asynchronous startup.

steps.title: Encode PCM into Opus
steps.text: The shared codec handles frame encoding/decoding. Browser wrappers call C/WASM while native callers use the same codec helpers directly.

chapters.title: Transmit and mix
chapters.summary: Hosts track sources and prepare recipient-specific output excluding the receiver’s own input.

steps.title: Batch native upload
steps.text: Capture and send work are separated so device timing is not directly blocked by every network write.

steps.title: Mix dedicated-server output
steps.text: The server mixes sources per recipient and encodes outgoing Opus. Excluding the listener avoids sending their voice back over the network.

steps.title: Mix shared-session sources
steps.text: Per-source writes and exclude-a-participant mixing belong to shared session audio. This is distinct from acoustic echo cancellation on a device.

chapters.title: Decode, buffer, and play
chapters.summary: After receipt, samples still require decoding, pacing, and a live output device.

steps.title: Decode native audio
steps.text: Batch structure is validated before Opus frames are decoded and samples forwarded to playback processing.

steps.title: Process native duplex audio
steps.text: The C++ client pipeline integrates WebRTC AEC3. Playback-reference and capture processing address speaker-to-microphone echo.

steps.title: Drain browser PCM
steps.text: The worklet drains queued samples and reports underruns. AudioPipeline owns its lifetime, decoder integration, and speaker choice.

views.title: Share files & streams
views.question: I want a clip, image, GIF, or URL instead of my camera.
views.goal: Compare native FFmpeg/yt-dlp resolution with browser playback, GIF composition, and container fallback.
views.subtitle: Compare native FFmpeg/yt-dlp resolution with browser playback, GIF composition, and container fallback.
views.outcome: Identify who owns decoding/audio and how resulting frames re-enter preview or call upload.
views.diagnostic: Native URL extraction and browser container fallback have different owners: yt-dlp resolves supported sites, while browser fallback can transcode unsupported containers locally.

chapters.title: Resolve native sources
chapters.summary: File and URL choices enter the source layer before ordinary capture.

steps.title: Apply source options
steps.text: The shared lifecycle reads file/URL choices, probes timing, and configures capture for mirror, client, or discovery.

steps.title: Choose direct or extracted input
steps.text: Native extensions/direct streams can go straight to FFmpeg. Other supported site URLs can first resolve through yt-dlp.

steps.title: Decode media
steps.text: FFmpeg owns selected input, codec state, seek/timing, and decoded frames. It does not itself choose final ASCII glyphs.

chapters.title: Decode browser uploads
chapters.summary: Ordinary media elements and source-specific fallbacks converge on reusable frame capture.

steps.title: Own upload lifetime
steps.text: Object URLs, media kind, cancellation, playback controls, and cleanup live here. Ordinary browser video/audio playback stays in media elements.

steps.title: Composite GIF animation
steps.text: Frame composition and disposal rules preserve GIF animation rather than assuming one image draw will animate it.

steps.title: Convert unsupported containers
steps.text: Fallback loads FFmpeg WASM and produces browser-playable media for supported fallback containers. It is separate from native FFmpeg decoding.

chapters.title: Reuse rendering and upload
chapters.summary: Changing a source should not create another ASCII converter or packet format.

steps.title: Capture decoded pixels
steps.text: The canvas bridge reads active media into the pixel representation consumed by rendering/upload paths.

steps.title: Preview through C/WASM
steps.text: Uploaded frames enter the normal C converter. Browser playback can preserve audible file audio independently of visual conversion.

steps.title: Share into a call
steps.text: The client page coordinates selected media with outgoing video/audio. Local Mirror playback alone is not a network send.

views.title: Change controls & settings
views.question: I want to resize, mute, change colors, or share a configured link.
views.goal: Follow native precedence, browser URL state, C option setters, live keys, and receiver capability updates.
views.subtitle: Follow native precedence, browser URL state, C option setters, live keys, and receiver capability updates.
views.outcome: Separate local rendering preferences from values that must reach the host, and find device/private-link state.
views.diagnostic: If a widget updates without changing output, follow its state-to-WASM setter and any capability/settings packet. URL state alone does not prove C has applied the value.

chapters.title: Resolve values
chapters.summary: Native options and browser URL state enter different adapters before C runtime use.

steps.title: Resolve native configuration
steps.text: Mode defaults, configuration/environment values, explicit arguments, validation, and publication happen in the option system.

steps.title: Manage URL-backed settings
steps.text: Shared links and refresh restoration are explicit state operations. Restoring a link does not grant device permission again.

steps.title: Serialize shareable state
steps.text: The utility omits default scalar values and handles dedicated fragment fields for private values. Inspect it before changing invitation links.

chapters.title: Apply live settings
chapters.summary: React values become C options through explicit adapters.

steps.title: Render available controls
steps.text: Browser controls expose binary-style values. The UI layer describes values while settings adapters apply them.

steps.title: Call C-facing setters
steps.text: UI values and dimensions are translated into module settings. Initialization gates prevent writes before a usable module exists.

steps.title: Publish consistent options
steps.text: The shared options store serves runtime readers and writers. A cached React value differs from the published option state consumed by C.

chapters.title: Route live actions
chapters.summary: Local presentation and host-generated output require different update paths.

steps.title: Apply native actions
steps.text: Mute, pause, help, and display actions route through session controls/options rather than raw terminal text.

steps.title: Advertise receiver capabilities
steps.text: Dimensions, colors/styles, FPS, and codec support are sent to the host and affect the output it generates.

steps.title: Apply session settings
steps.text: Shared settings have explicit serialization, version comparison, and option application. This boundary differs from a local widget.

views.title: Recover & hand off a call
views.question: What happens if the network or current host disappears?
views.goal: Separate retry, stream liveness, host selection, handoff generations, and retirement of stale media work.
views.subtitle: Separate retry, stream liveness, host selection, handoff generations, and retirement of stale media work.
views.outcome: Find executable handoff code and distinguish it from illustrative consensus integration helpers.
views.diagnostic: Identify the failed layer first: signaling, media channel, stream delivery, or host ownership. A socket reconnect does not itself elect a host or cancel stale capture work.

chapters.title: Retry the right session
chapters.summary: Native client and browser hook maintain different retry/liveness policies.

steps.title: Back off native retries
steps.text: Connection retries use a bounded delay. Client policy, shutdown state, and remote errors determine whether another attempt should occur.

steps.title: Watch stream and connection state
steps.text: Attempts reset on connection. Stream-stall timing starts after a real frame, and host creation is not treated like an ordinary reconnectable join.

steps.title: Detect media-channel loss
steps.text: The joining strategy has peer timers alongside its signaling connection. A working signaling socket does not prove the media DataChannel survived.

chapters.title: Transfer host ownership
chapters.summary: The active protocol validates session identity, generations, and staged role changes.

steps.title: Schedule samples and commits
steps.text: The browser emits measurements and processes preparation/commit actions. C validates wire structure; browser scheduling does not replace the C selector.

steps.title: Apply native role changes
steps.text: Discovery consumes handoff state and changes host/participant ownership while managing transports.

steps.title: Coordinate service-side handoff
steps.text: The service uses session/migration state to coordinate a new host. consensus_integration.c contains illustrative placeholders and is not substituted for this active path.

chapters.title: Retire stale work
chapters.summary: Async device startup and role changes need explicit ownership checks during recovery.

steps.title: Invalidate native generations
steps.text: Generation, active-work, and stop-completion state let late results be recognized as stale.

steps.title: Check browser generations
steps.text: Audio/media adapters use C-backed generation state so an old async start cannot take ownership after disconnect or device replacement.

steps.title: Adopt or release hosting
steps.text: A promoted browser can adopt existing signaling/membership. Timers, decoders, peers, and the C host instance must follow one teardown lifecycle.

views.title: Snapshot, record & diagnose
views.question: I want reproducible output, or need to find why a call failed.
views.goal: Follow snapshot timing, terminal-to-video export, encoder drain, and filtered logging that preserves the UI.
views.subtitle: Follow snapshot timing, terminal-to-video export, encoder drain, and filtered logging that preserves the UI.
views.outcome: Locate first-frame timing, render-file lifetime, and logs at the failing connection or media stage.
views.diagnostic: Process exit does not prove export finalization. Follow queued frames into drain/flush and container completion; correlate live logs with the specific failing stage.

chapters.title: Capture the intended interval
chapters.summary: Snapshot timing is tied to real frames rather than a fixed startup sleep.

steps.title: Use ordinary setup
steps.text: Snapshots and render-file choices still pass through normal mirror/client-like source and display initialization.

steps.title: Wait for the actual frame
steps.text: Immediate snapshots must produce a frame before exit. Callback-driven rendering checks completion while local capture can use the pipeline.

steps.title: Track output timing
steps.text: Display tracks frame output and snapshot/render timing. Dimensions and TTY status alter presentation behavior.

chapters.title: Turn terminal frames into video
chapters.summary: Export rasterizes terminal output; it is not simply saving the original webcam stream.

steps.title: Own the export context
steps.text: Display chooses dimensions, FPS, theme, and output options, then owns the render-file context.

steps.title: Rasterize ANSI
steps.text: Terminal parsing and glyph rendering produce pixels for each exported frame.

steps.title: Encode and finalize
steps.text: FFmpeg writes rendered pixels and audio. Render-file teardown drains pending output and finalizes the output container.

chapters.title: Inspect the right boundary
chapters.summary: Logging and screen composition share infrastructure instead of competing for terminal output.

steps.title: Filter relevant events
steps.text: Select connection, handshake, capture, or frame messages to expose one boundary without changing media behavior.

steps.title: Collect screen logs
steps.text: Session screens consume a recent-log buffer rather than letting raw debug printing interrupt terminal rendering.

steps.title: Compare host activity
steps.text: Counters add context for admission, receive, render, and send work. They do not replace checking that the receiver actually presented frames.
